title: Open Model Selection Lab & Compatibility Walkthrough
next_steps: Send model-compatibility spreadsheet and kernel mapping - Maya
Share SOC2 + deployment checklist - Maya to Priya
Schedule 2-hour POC scoping with infra + ML team - Rafael to propose times
action_items: Maya Chen - Send pricing tiers and Dedicated capacity options - due 2025-09-08
Rafael Ortiz - Export short benchmark run (latency & cost) for 3 candidate models - due 2025-09-10
Priya Desai - Provide compliance questionnaire answers for Private deployment - due 2025-09-12
summary: Introductory lab-style demo of Redwood's model catalog, benchmark interpretation, and compatibility matrix for BrightPath Health. Focus on picking an open model candidate for chat/triage, tradeoffs between hosted vs Dedicated vs Private, and kernel/hardware compatibility. Customer wants data residency and SOC2 notes; agreed to run a POC and share benchmark artifacts.
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya, AE on the account. Rafael from SE will drive the demo, and Lena's here for architecture Qs.
[00:12] Dr. Anika Sahu: Hi thanks, Anika here. We're most interested in picking an open model for patient triage chat, low latency, and also we need to understand private deploy options.
[00:20] Tom Rivera: Hey Tom, platform. We'll care about latencies under 200ms p95 for short messages and also cost per 1k requests.
[00:28] Rafael Ortiz: Great, we'll walk through the catalog start to finish. Quick caveat: some of the auto-transcription labels may be off, so Rafael might get tagged as Speaker 2 later.
[00:36] [00:36] Rafael Ortiz: Okay, starting the Redwood Console — top left is the model catalog. We surface curated open models, and we surface a "compatibility" column which is a short-hand: architecture, quantization-friendly, and kernel mappings.
[00:52] Dr. Anika Sahu: Question, when you say compatibility, is that per GPU vendor? We run on-prem for PHI.
[00:58] Lena Park: Good question. The compatibility flags include hardware targets (A100, H100, T4-like), and runtime kernels — but for Private we also run a small detection pass to map to the customer's available kernels.
[01:10] [01:10] Priya Desai: From compliance — we need to know what data is logged. Is KV cache persisted? Where are logs stored?
[01:18] Rafael Ortiz: Short answer: logs are configurable. For Private you control the control plane and can opt out of message retention; the default hosted path retains minimal telemetry for billing. We'll send the retention table.
[01:26] Maya Chen: I'll drop the SOC2 packet and the deployment checklist after the call.
[01:32] [01:32] Rafael Ortiz: Back to catalog: here's a model tile for "open-llm-med-3b" — it's an example we often recommend for low-latency triage. Benchmarks to the right show throughput and p95 latency under our hosted profile.
[01:44] Tom Rivera: Are those bench numbers on H100?
[01:46] Rafael Ortiz: This column mixes our verified runs. The label says "H100/FP16 / batch size 8 / seq 128". The console also links the raw bench CSV. Note that quantizaton changes both latency and token cost.
[01:58] Dr. Anika Sahu: We saw an internal note about prefix KV caching to speed up subsequent messages. Can you demo that?
[02:06] Rafael Ortiz: Sure — in Optimize there's an option to enable prefix caching per-route. If the triage bot often uses the same system prompt and a fixed context, you cache KV state which reduces the per-request compute by skipping repeated attention compute.
[02:20] [02:20] Speaker 4: Sorry, quick clarification: is the KV cache encrypted at rest?
[02:24] Rafael Ortiz: Yes for Private deployments we integrate with customer KMS; for Hosted we encrypt with our managed keys but can also bring your own key for Dedicated.
[02:34] Maya Chen: (faint) I'll note the KMS options in the follow-up.
[02:38] [02:38] Rafael Ortiz: Next is the compatibility matrix. This is a cross-reference: model variant, kernel family (fused-attention v2, flash-attn variant), and hardware target.
[02:50] Dr. Anika Sahu: What's an example mismatch?
[02:52] Rafael Ortiz: An example: a 7B model might be listed as "H100-optimized" but on older T4-like cards you'd fallback to a slower kernel path; throughput drops and latency may double. The matrix tells you which kernels are available and expected perf.
[03:06] [03:06] Tom Rivera: So if we pick open-llm-med-3b and run on our A100 racks, should we expect similar numbers to the console?
[03:12] Rafael Ortiz: Generally yes, within noise — provided your CUDA/NCCL stack and drivers match our tested versions. For Private we run a small smoke benchmark to confirm. We'll include that script.
[03:22] [03:22] Dr. Anika Sahu: Can we get a smaller memory footprint model? We have memory constraints per node.
[03:28] Rafael Ortiz: Yes, we can show quantized variants: q4f16/q4_0 depending on model—these trade a small quality delta for big memory savings. There's a quantization compatibility column in the catalog.
[03:40] [03:40] Priya Desai: From compliance side — any impact on hallucination rates with quantization? We need high precision for medical content.
[03:48] Rafael Ortiz: Great point. Quantization can slightly affect generation fidelity; part of our Optimize toolkit runs targeted evals (bleu/accuracy style or domain-specific prompts) to measure regressions. We recommend running your clinical prompt-set to validate.
[04:02] [04:02] Rafael Ortiz: I'll open the bench viewer: here's a scatter plot of latency vs cost per 1k tokens across models. You can filter by model size, kernel, and hardware.
[04:12] Dr. Anika Sahu: Nice. Can we export those bench CSVs?
[04:15] Rafael Ortiz: Yep export button top right.
[04:18] [04:18] Maya Chen: (typing) I'll attach the sample CSV to the follow-up with annotations.
[04:24] [04:24] Rafael Ortiz: Now routing policies — you can route by SLA: low-latency routes prefer H100-backed pools; cost-sensitive routes go to quantized variants on cheaper GPUs; fallback policies can route to a smaller model if the main pool is saturated.
[04:40] Tom Rivera: If there's an outage, can the fallback still respect data residency?
[04:44] Lena Park: If you use Private, routing is within your VPC so residency is preserved. For Hosted route fallbacks might cross regions unless you strict-route; that's a config and we can lock it down.
[04:58] [04:58] Priya Desai: Also need audit logs of who accessed what model and prompt. Is that available?
[05:04] Rafael Ortiz: Yes, Console has audit trails: per-request logging, user-level access records, and model-version changes. These are exportable to your SIEM.
[05:12] [05:12] Dr. Anika Sahu: Walk me through a practical selection workflow — how do you pick 2-3 candidates?
[05:18] Rafael Ortiz: We usually start with constraints: memory footprint, latency target, and quality requirements. Step one: filter catalog by hardware compatibility and quantization support. Step two: run a small benchmark for latency/cost. Step three: run your eval prompts in Optimize for quality regression. Then pick final candidate(s) and pilot in Dedicated or Private.
[05:38] [05:38] Tom Rivera: How long is a typical POC?
[05:40] Maya Chen: POCs are typically 4–8 weeks depending on integration depth; a smoke bench + eval + a limited pilot can be done in 2–3 weeks if infra is ready.
[05:50] [05:50] Priya Desai: For legal, we need contract language about data handling during POC.
[05:54] Maya Chen: We'll share standard POC terms and highlight the Private path where data never leaves your VPC.
[05:59] [05:59] Speaker 4: There's a quick micro-demo request: can you show the model variant compare UI?
[06:04] Rafael Ortiz: Sure — selecting two variants side-by-side, you get token cost, p95 latency, and a sample QA output. Note: the sample inference sometimes uses a synthetic prompt and the transcription might have minor errors in product names.
[06:18] Dr. Anika Sahu: The sample output looks good for common triage flows. How do we lock a model version?
[06:24] Rafael Ortiz: In the Console you pin model version and then create a rollout policy; canary % and automatic rollback on quality regressions is supported.
[06:34] [06:34] Tom Rivera: Any limitations on model sizes for Private?
[06:36] Lena Park: Only infra bounds: if your nodes don't have enough GPU RAM, you can't run very large weights without model parallelism. We can recommend a pack/unpack config or split across multiple GPUs if needed.
[06:48] Rafael Ortiz: Okay, quick demo of a bench export and then I'll open the kernel-mapping doc. Here's a direct link to a kernel mapping spreadsheet (shared link). It shows fused-attention variants and which models use them.
[06:58] [06:58] Dr. Anika Sahu: Good — please share that.
[07:00] Maya Chen: Noted. We'll include kernel mapping and the driver matrix.
[07:06] [07:06] Rafael Ortiz: Wrapping up — main recommended next steps: we suggest running a short latency benchmark on your A100 nodes with open-llm-med-3b quantized and non-quantized, and run 300 clinical prompts through Optimize to measure quality delta.
[07:22] Priya Desai: I'll coordinate on the clinical prompt-set.
[07:26] Maya Chen: Great. Any final questions?
[07:30] [07:30] Dr. Anika Sahu: One last: pricing for Dedicated vs Hosted for production?
[07:33] Maya Chen: I'll send a tailored pricing sheet. Dedicated is reserved capacity so we provide committed reductions; Hosted is pay-as-you-go.
[07:42] Rafael Ortiz: And if you go Private, we'll work with your infra team for sizing and give a one-time deployment fee estimate.
[07:50] [07:50] Maya Chen: Okay, we'll follow up with the artefacts discussed: SOC2, kernel mapping, bench CSV, pricing, and POC times. Thanks everyone.
[07:58] Tom Rivera: Thanks all.
[08:00] [End of recording]
